question: In recent days, we witnessed the crime against refugees and migrants in Chios and the tragedy off the coast of Crete. The latest developments, with the wider flare-up in the Middle East, are proof that the worst is yet to come. The regulation adopted by the European Parliament provides for very tough penalties for asylum seekers whose applications are rejected and who refuse to leave the territory of the EU.

It also provides for the mutual recognition of decisions by any Member State, putting an end to the haggling over ‘secondary movements’ and how to share the burden of deportations. In view of the above, will the Commission state its views on: 1.

the fact that the alleged reduction in refugee and migrant arrivals is nothing more than the result of an intensified crackdown, which has reached a whole new level now with the so-called return hubs, namely the inhumane centres for the expulsion and deportation of uprooted persons to non-EU countries, approved also by the European Parliament, and which concern a policy that is directly linked to the largest number of victims recorded in the Mediterranean Sea in the last decade?

the fact that the Nea Dimokratia Government was quick to suspend decisions on Iranian asylum applications, as it had done previously with Syrians from the EU, looking ahead and preventing the big victims, namely uprooted people, from fleeing war in the Middle East, a war that is supported by Nea Dimokratia and the EU and in which they are both are implicated?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (29.6.2026) The Commission and the Member States have been working closely together and with key partner countries to reduce illegal migration to the EU, including by preventing dangerous journeys and loss of lives, improving migration management both in the EU and in partner countries, and promoting globally the respect of migrants and refugees’ rights.

The combination of the new rules of the Pact on Migration and Asylum, migration diplomacy, and operational cooperation within and outside the EU is showing results, notably with a significant reduction in illegal arrivals since 2023. The Return Regulation, on which the EU legislators have reached a political agreement, will complement the Pact rules.

It establishes a new legal framework with swifter, simpler and more effective return procedures across the EU that respect fundamental rights and international obligations, notably the principle of non-refoulement. The Regulation provides the legal framework to establish ‘return hubs’ outside the EU, subject to specific conditions and safeguards, including human rights guarantees.

The Commission recalls that Member States must implement asylum and migration rules in compliance with their obligations under EU law, including the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU. The Commission remains in close contact with the Greek authorities regarding the implementation of the relevant EU rules in this area.
